story.title: Why the Seasons Come Around
story.story: At noon, the stick's shadow was shorter than it had been last month. A child in the village had been marking the tip of that shadow with a pebble every week. The pebbles made a curve across the dirt. Why did the sun climb so high in summer? Why did it sink so low in winter? The child asked a teacher one afternoon. She carried an orange and a lamp into the classroom. She pushed a pin through the orange, from the top to the bottom. That pin stood for the axis, an invisible line that Earth spins around. Earth does not stand straight up as it travels around the sun. It leans over, tipped about twenty-three and a half degrees. A degree is a small unit for measuring how far something tips. The teacher placed the lamp in the middle of the room. The lamp stood for the sun. She walked the orange in a slow circle around the lamp. She kept the pin tipped the same way the whole time. When the top leaned toward the lamp, that half got straighter light. Straighter light is packed into a smaller space, so that half feels warmer. That half also had longer days, since the sun stayed up for more hours. That is summer. On the far side of the circle, the top leaned away. Light arrived at a slant and spread thin over more ground. Days grew short and cool. That is winter. The child stood very still, watching the orange turn. Then the child remembered the pebbles in the dirt. They curved up and down, following the sun's path across the sky. Many people guess that the sun must move closer to Earth in summer. That guess is natural, but it is not the reason. Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January, during northern winter. The tilt is the real reason. The tilt points the same way all year as Earth travels around. So each half takes its turn leaning toward the sun. The child picked up the last pebble and smiled. Next week, the shadow would be a little longer. And now the child knew why.
